universe.scoring: Scores are percentiles within this universe (0 = lowest repo, 100 = highest; ties share the average rank), and a criterion built from several metrics is the mean of their percentiles, rounded to 0.1. Higher always means more of the criterion. Popularity: stars. Momentum: lifetime star velocity (stars_per_day) and forks created in the last 30 days (forks_30d), equally weighted (D13; star_events_30d is not used because the events feed caps it). Quality: commits in the last 90 days, distinct commit authors in the last 90 days, number of releases, recency of the last commit, and README length, equally weighted, so an active, multi-author, released and documented repo scores high. Newness: creation date, so the newest repo scores 100. A metric that is unknown (None) for a repo counts as the median (50) for that repo, neither rewarded nor penalised; the other repos' percentiles are computed among the known values only.

# Holon

English | [中文](README.zh-CN.md)

[![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/holon-run/holon?sort=semver)](https://github.com/holon-run/holon/releases/latest)[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-Apache--2.0-blue.svg)](LICENSE)

**Create and run AI assistants on your own computer or server.**

Holon is open-source software for individuals and teams to create and run AI assistants on their own computers or servers. Assign tasks to your assistants, track their progress, and let them follow up on ongoing work.

## What does Holon provide?

| Capability | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Continuous agent workspace** | Each agent has its own continuous working context in Holon, instead of restarting with every terminal, request, or client connection. |
| **Work-first task model** | Holon organizes tasks, waits, execution progress, and final delivery as explicit Work, instead of leaving them scattered across conversations. |
| **Event-driven wait and wake** | Agents can wait for task results, external events, or operator input, then return to the corresponding work when the condition is satisfied. |
| **Explicit context and trust boundaries** | Holon distinguishes operator input, external events, tool results, and internal execution traces so information from different origins is not mixed together. |
| **Local-first execution environment** | Holon is built for local repositories, shell, worktrees, and development toolchains, letting agents execute tasks in the real working environment. |

> Keep agent work alive in your local workspace.

## Quickstart

Holon provides two interaction modes: **TUI** (terminal) and **Web GUI** (browser).

### 1. Install

```bash
brew tap holon-run/tap && brew install holon
```

Or download binaries from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/holon-run/holon/releases/latest).

### 2. Configure a provider

```bash
holon onboard
```

This walks through provider credential setup interactively. You can also
configure providers through the Web GUI **Settings** page after starting the
daemon. See [Configuration Reference](docs/website/reference/configuration.md)
and [Web GUI guide](docs/website/guides/use-web-gui.md) for more.

### 3. Start the daemon

```bash
holon daemon start
```

### 4a. TUI (terminal)

```bash
holon tui
```

Select an agent and start working. Agents keep running after you disconnect.

### 4b. Web GUI (browser)

Open <http://localhost:7878>. Create an agent and work through a chat interface
with built-in file browser, task tracking, and more.

For more: [TUI guide](docs/website/reference/tui.md) · [Web GUI guide](docs/website/guides/use-web-gui.md) · [First agent](docs/website/getting-started/first-agent.md)

## Local App reference

The reference Local App fixture lives in
`examples/local-app/agent-workbench`. Copy it into an Agent's
`agent_home/apps/` directory as `agent-workbench`, start Holon, and open:

```text
/apps/<agent-id>/agent-workbench/
```

It demonstrates the Local App lifecycle: discovery, static HTML/CSS/JavaScript
hosting, `Holon.context()`, `Holon.request()`, and `Holon.events`. The
end-to-end fixture test can be run with:

```bash
cargo test --test http_apps apps_reference_workbench_end_to_end
```

Hosted apps load the browser artifact from
`/apps/<agent-id>/<app-id>/holon.js`. The artifact installs `window.Holon` and
uses the existing same-origin session boundary; App requests do not become
operator input and do not grant additional permissions.

## Install

```bash
brew tap holon-run/tap
brew install holon
holon --help
```

You can also download prebuilt binaries for Linux amd64, macOS amd64, and macOS
arm64 from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/holon-run/holon/releases/latest).
The Linux amd64 binary supports Ubuntu 22.04 or newer (glibc 2.35 or newer).

macOS 13 or later users on Apple Silicon or Intel Macs can install the
universal `Holon-<version>.dmg` from the same release page. The native menu
bar app controls the same daemon as the CLI, supports
launch at login, and can install its bundled CLI into `~/.local/bin` without
overwriting another installation.

The examples below assume `holon` is installed on `PATH`.

### Docker

Release images are published to GitHub Container Registry. The container runs
`holon serve` in the foreground and requires a control token because it listens
on a non-loopback address:

```bash
docker run --rm \
  -p 127.0.0.1:7878:7878 \
  -e HOLON_CONTROL_TOKEN='replace-with-a-long-random-token' \
  -e HOLON_MODEL='openai/gpt-5.4' \
  -e OPENAI_API_KEY \
  -v holon-home:/var/lib/holon \
  ghcr.io/holon-run/holon:latest
```

Replace the model and credential environment variable when using another
provider. Holon validates that the configured model provider is available
before the service starts. Scheduling is canonical-only. A legacy selector is
rejected at startup; use Holon v0.31.1 with a pre-migration database backup if
legacy rollback is required.

Bake'n Deck bakes each one into the files themselves: | Subcommand | The gap it fills | What it does | |---|---|---| | [`baken headroom`](#loudness-normalizer-baken-headroom) | Auto Gain is ignored on USB export | Measures LUFS / True Peak and bakes safe gain into the audio file — **no limiter**, dynamics preserved, cues stay linked | | [`baken rbsort`](#rekordbox-playlist-sorter-baken-rbsort) | No compound Key+BPM sort in rekordbox | Sorts every playlist by **Alphanumeric key (1A→12B) then BPM** inside your exported XML — CDJs play it in that exact order | | [`baken cdjsafe`](#cdj-safe-transcoder-baken-cdjsafe) | Pre-NXS2 CDJs only play MP3 reliably | Transcodes whole playlists to **320 kbps CBR MP3** with **cues and beatgrid carried over** — the emergency-backup USB | | [`baken expressport`](#direct-usb-export-baken-expressport) | Exporting to USB means launching rekordbox and waiting | **Writes the stick directly** from the `collection.xml` rekordbox exports: device library, rekordbox's own analysis files, audio, My Settings | 🌐 **[baken.ravers.workers.dev](https://baken.ravers.workers.dev)** — full docs, workflow guides, and FAQ. ## Built for rekordbox, not instead of it There is no shortage of tools that set out to replace rekordbox. Bake'n Deck is not one of them. rekordbox is where you analyse tracks, set beat grids and cues, build playlists and keep your library. Bake'n Deck takes on only the few steps rekordbox leaves out of the trip to the CDJ, and it goes through the doors rekordbox itself provides. - **Your library stays in rekordbox.** Every subcommand works on the collection XML rekordbox exports, and results go back through rekordbox's own Imported Library (the `rekordbox xml` tree). Nothing to migrate, nothing to sync back. - **rekordbox's database is never touched.** Its `master.db` is never read, decrypted or written. - **rekordbox's own analysis is copied, not re-guessed.** On a stick, the waveforms and phrases are rekordbox's analysis files, byte for byte apart from the rewrites rekordbox itself makes at export time. Analysis is generated only for tracks rekordbox has never seen, and only when you ask for it. - **Measured, not guessed.** The stick format was worked out from real rekordbox 7 exports and is checked against them byte for byte. Player limits come from Pioneer DJ's operating instructions only, cited page by page. Whatever has not been measured or tried on a player is labelled as such. - **Tried on real CDJs.** DJs have played sticks written by `baken` on a CDJ-3000, CDJ-2000NXS2 players and a CDJ-2000NXS ([#116](https://github.com/M-Igashi/baken/issues/116), [#242](https://github.com/M-Igashi/baken/issues/242)). Where rekordbox is still the safer route, the docs say so. - **Supply chain, handled with care.** A tool that rewrites your music library and writes your gig stick has to be trustworthy down to its dependencies. Each new dependency is weighed before it comes in: SQLCipher and a vendored OpenSSL were dropped in 4.6.0, and on Apple platforms the encryption uses the operating system's own CommonCrypto since 4.6.1. Every pull request goes through dependency review, which fails on a known vulnerability of moderate severity or higher, and a licence check stops the build on any licence not on the accepted list. Every GitHub Action is pinned to a full commit SHA and workflows are read-only unless a job needs more; crates.io releases use Trusted Publishing, so no crates.io token is stored anywhere. Release archives carry SHA-256 checksums. - **The DJ decides.** Bake'n Deck reports facts and leaves the call to you: a suspect file is flagged, not quietly fixed, and no feature, AI or otherwise, takes over a decision that belongs to the DJ. ## Bake'n Deck for Mac [**Bake'n Deck for Mac**](https://apps.apple.com/app/baken-deck/id6808813823) is the native app edition, on the Mac App Store. txcript is a library for converting agent sessions. Start a conversation in Claude Code and continue it in Codex, carrying over messages, reasoning, and tool history where the target supports them. Build session search, viewers, and editors against one transcript model. txcript handles the agent-specific formats, with a Rust API, a JavaScript package, and a CLI. [Try the CLI](#try-the-cli) · [Use the library](#use-the-library) · [Supported agents](#supported-agents) · [Documentation](#documentation)

## Try the CLI Download a binary for macOS, Linux, or Windows from [Releases](https://github.com/skillsynchq/txcript/releases), or install from source with Rust 1.96 or newer: ```sh cargo install --git https://github.com/skillsynchq/txcript txcript-cli --locked ``` Find a Claude Code session and continue it in Codex: ```sh txcript list --from claude_code txcript continue --with codex ``` Use an ID from the list; an unambiguous prefix works too. txcript writes a new native session and launches Codex in the recorded working directory. The source session is kept. Have the target agent installed and signed in before continuing. Other ways to work with your sessions: ```sh txcript query "relay bug" # search local session history txcript view # read a conversation in the terminal txcript crop # edit or trim history into a new copy txcript export --out run.json ``` Move `run.json` to another machine and continue it with `txcript continue ./run.json --with claude_code`. Bring the project files separately. Run `txcript mcp` to let an MCP client list, search, and read past sessions. Its tools are read-only. See the [CLI reference](docs/usage.md#cli) for filters, message ranges, and shell integration. ## Use the library ### Rust ```sh cargo add txcript ``` Convert a Claude Code transcript into Codex's native format: ```rust use txcript::harness::{claude_code::ClaudeCode, codex::Codex}; use txcript::{TextCodec, convert}; fn main() -> Result<(), Box> { let input = std::fs::read_to_string("session.jsonl")?; let source = ClaudeCode::from_text(&input)?; let target = convert::(&source)?; std::fs::write("rollout.jsonl", Codex::to_text(&target)?)?; Ok(()) } ``` Use `Store` implementations to discover, load, and save sessions in an agent's own storage. Convert to `Transcript` to search, crop, or render conversations through the same API across agents. See the [Rust API](https://docs.rs/txcript) and [examples](docs/usage.md#rust-crate). ### JavaScript ```sh npm install txcript ``` ```js import { convert } from "txcript"; import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs"; const input = readFileSync("session.jsonl", "utf8"); const output = convert(input, "claude_code", "codex"); writeFileSync("rollout.jsonl", output); ``` The package includes prebuilt WebAssembly for Node and Bun. It converts and searches session text in memory; your application handles files and storage. See the [JavaScript reference](docs/usage.md#npm

Muxin

One app for all your machines, run by you or by your AI agents.
muxin.dev · free and open source (Apache-2.0)

Point it at the machines you own (a Mac Studio under the desk, a NUC, a Linux box, a few MacBooks, a Windows laptop) and Muxin becomes the hub for all of them: - **Agent sessions:** Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Amp, Pi or a shell on any machine, in a real terminal, still running after you close the app. - **Boxes:** hand a task to an agent that works on it by itself, in a container of its own on one of your machines. A box pauses when it's quiet and picks up where it left off when you ask it more. - **Desktops:** see a Linux machine's screen live and use it, beside an agent's terminal or in its own window. - **Files and clipboard:** copy files and folders between any two machines, and copy on your Mac to paste on a machine (and back). - **GitHub:** your inbox, repositories, issues and pull requests, with one click to hand an issue to an agent on the machine you pick. - **Self-hosted runners:** which runners are working, idle or offline, which jobs no runner can take, and installing, starting, stopping or removing runners. - **Health:** CPU, memory, disk and uptime, and a plain answer when a machine is offline or unreachable. Agents can also **borrow a machine as a work environment**: an [agent workspace](#agent-workspaces) is a persistent folder (optionally a git checkout) on one of your machines where an agent runs commands, edits files and syncs code. - **Native and fast.** The window is built with [GPUI](https://www.gpui.rs), the GPU-accelerated UI framework behind the Zed editor. It runs on macOS, Linux and Windows. - **Agent-first.** Every capability is available as an MCP server (`muxin mcp`) and as scriptable commands with `--json`. Claude Code, Codex and other agents can check your machines, explain problems and fix them. - **Uses what you already have.** Machines are first reached with your system `ssh`, so your keys, agent and `~/.ssh/config` aliases just work; after that Muxin talks to its own small agent there, directly or through [Tailscale](#tailscale-and-moving-between-networks). GitHub access uses your `gh` login. ## Install Download the app from the [latest release](https://github.com/LumaryLabsLLC/muxin/releases/latest): - **macOS** 12 or later, Apple silicon and Intel: `Muxin--macos.dmg`. Open it and drag Muxin to Applications. It's signed and notarized. - **Linux** with glibc 2.35 or newer (Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12, Fedora 36, openSUSE Tumbleweed, RHEL 10 and later), for Intel and AMD (`x86_64`) or Arm (`aarch64`): - Debian and Ubuntu: `Muxin--linux-x86_64.deb`, then `sudo apt install ./Muxin--linux-x86_64.deb`. - Fedora, openSUSE and RHEL: `Muxin--linux-x86_64.rpm`, then `sudo dnf install ./Muxin--linux-x86_64.rpm` (or `zypper install`). - Arch: `yay -S muxin-bin` from the [AUR](https://aur.archlinux.org/packages/muxin-bin), or `Muxin--linux-x86_64.pkg.tar.zst` with `sudo pacman -U`. - Any distribution: `Muxin--linux-x86_64.AppImage`. Make it executable and run it; it needs no FUSE 2. - Or `Muxin--linux-x86_64.tar.gz`: unpack it and run `./Muxin/install.sh`, which installs it for you, no root needed. - **Windows 11**: `Muxin--windows-x64-setup.exe`, or `windows-arm64` on Windows on Arm. The installer isn't signed yet, so Windows may say "Windows protected your PC": click **More info**, then **Run anyway**. Or with [Homebrew](https://brew.sh), on macOS and Linux: ```sh brew install --cask lumarylabsllc/tap/muxin ``` `SHA256SUMS.txt` in each release has the files' checksums. Muxin tells you when a new version is out: the sidebar says so, and About shows how to update the copy you have (with Homebrew or the AUR, or the new file to download). It asks GitHub for the latest release when it opens and twice a day; turn that off in **Settings › General › Updates**. `muxin updates` checks from a terminal. Muxin was called Muxen before 0.5.1. Updating keeps your settings, machines and sessions, and the `muxen` command still works. On a Mac, the old Muxen app goes to the Trash the first time Muxin opens. ### Build from source ```sh git clone https://github.com/LumaryLabsLLC/muxin && cd muxin cargo build --release --workspace ./target/release/muxin # opens the window ``` `--workspace` also builds Muxin's agent for this computer, which the app sets up on it. # mcpls

[![Crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/mcpls?label=mcpls)](https://crates.io/crates/mcpls)
[![docs.rs](https://img.shields.io/docsrs/mcpls-core?label=mcpls-core)](https://docs.rs/mcpls-core)
[![CI](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/bug-ops/mcpls/ci.yml?branch=main)](https://github.com/bug-ops/mcpls/actions)
[![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/bug-ops/mcpls/graph/badge.svg?token=FQEDLNF2GS)](https://codecov.io/gh/bug-ops/mcpls)
[![MSRV](https://img.shields.io/badge/MSRV-1.99-blue)](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/releases/tag/1.99.0)
[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT%2FApache--2.0-blue)](LICENSE-MIT)

**Give your AI coding agent a compiler's understanding of your code.**

mcpls is a bridge between the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and the Language Server Protocol (LSP). It runs the language servers for your project (rust-analyzer, pyright, gopls, and others) and exposes their type information, references, diagnostics and refactoring as 31 MCP tools, so an AI client reasons about code the way an IDE does.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C["AI client"] <-->|MCP| M["mcpls"] <-->|LSP| S["rust-analyzer / pyright / gopls / ..."]
```

## Documentation

The full documentation is the mcpls book: **<https://bug-ops.github.io/mcpls/>**

| Topic | Chapter |
|-------|---------|
| Install and first run | [Installation](https://bug-ops.github.io/mcpls/getting-started/installation.html) |
| Connect Claude Code or another client | [Connect an AI Client](https://bug-ops.github.io/mcpls/getting-started/connect-client.html) |
| Configure language servers | [Configuration](https://bug-ops.github.io/mcpls/guide/configuration.html) |
| All 31 tools | [Tools Overview](https://bug-ops.github.io/mcpls/tools/overview.html) |
| Something does not work | [Troubleshooting](https://bug-ops.github.io/mcpls/guide/troubleshooting.html) |
| HTTP transport and allowlists | [Transports](https://bug-ops.github.io/mcpls/advanced/transports.html) |
| Security model and untrusted workspaces | [Security and Trust](https://bug-ops.github.io/mcpls/advanced/security.html) |
| Every flag and config key | [Reference](https://bug-ops.github.io/mcpls/reference/cli.html) |

## Installation

**Linux and macOS:**

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bug-ops/mcpls/main/scripts/install.sh | sh
```

**Windows (PowerShell):**

```powershell
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bug-ops/mcpls/main/scripts/install.ps1 | iex
```

Or with Cargo:

```bash
cargo install mcpls
```

You also need at least one language server, for example `rustup component add rust-analyzer`. See [Installation](https://bug-ops.github.io/mcpls/getting-started/installation.html) for other methods and servers.

## Quick start

Register mcpls with Claude Code:

```bash
claude mcp add --scope user mcpls -- mcpls
```

Then ask about your code:

```text
You:    What is the return type of process_request?
Claude: [get_hover] It returns Result<Response, ApiError>.

You:    Find everywhere ApiError::Timeout is handled.
Claude: [get_references] Found 4 matches: src/handlers/api.rs:89, ...
```

Rust projects need no configuration. Other languages and clients are covered in the [book](https://bug-ops.github.io/mcpls/getting-started/minimal-config.html).

## Features

- **Type information and documentation** at any position
- **Cross-references, definitions, implementations** across the whole workspace
- **Real diagnostics** from the compiler, not guesses
- **Rename and code-action edits** returned for the client to apply
- **Call and type hierarchies**, symbol search, formatting, inlay hints, selection and folding ranges
- **Address code by symbol name** as well as by position, and restart language servers on demand
- **Several language servers at once**, started concurrently and stopped with mcpls, with graceful degradation when one fails
- **stdio by default**, optional HTTP transport with Host and Origin allowlists and resource subscriptions
- **Untrusted-workspace mode** for analyzing code you do not trust
- **Single Rust binary**, no runtime dependencies, no `unsafe` code

## Security

Language servers run code that comes with the workspace, and mcpls does not sandbox them. Read [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) and the [Security and Trust](https://bug-ops.github.io/mcpls/advanced/security.html) chapter before pointing mcpls at code you did not write.

## Agent skill

[`skills/mcpls`](skills/mcpls/) is a packaged [Agent Skill](https://agentskills.io/specification) that teaches an AI coding agent to install, configure and run mcpls.

## Development

```bash
cargo build
cargo nextest run --workspace --all-features
```

Requires Rust 1.99 or later (edition 2024). The book lives in [`book/`](book/) and is built with [mdBook](https://rust-lang.github.io/mdBook/). See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).

```sh
curl -fsSL https://cydonia.sh/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, `irm https://cydonia.sh/install.ps1 | iex`. To build from source,
`cargo install cydonia`.

## Where things live

```
~/.config/cydonia/   settings.toml, mcp.toml, the agent catalogue cache
~/.local/share/      installed agents
<project>/.cydonia/  that project's articles, boards, sessions and store
```

A project's own store carries a `.gitignore` — none of what cydonia writes
there is the project's source. More in
[Where things live](https://cydonia.sh/docs/general/files).

text: The evidence confirms five complementary sleepers: holon and baken are the clearest quality/value outliers; txcript has unusually strong momentum for its size; open-relay is a practical, well-developed agent-session utility; and mcpls is exceptionally under-popular for a documented, released developer integration. I’ll submit these five and rank all ten repositories inspected in detail.

**Crafting a pitch**

I'm thinking about how to create an effective one-line pitch that's under 200 characters. I want to make sure it expresses confidence. Next, I need to structure it in JSON format with exact scores for key figures. I'll include popularity scores as stars and use 30-day momentum metrics for forks. For maintenance, I'll reference a value of zero for mcpls and ensure quality commits are set to 90 days. Let's get this organized!

cards.pitch: A deeply active, released local-first agent workspace that remains only moderately discovered.

case.text: Holon combines continuous agent workspaces, explicit task/wait models, event-driven wake-up, trust boundaries, and local-first execution, with both TUI and web GUI workflows.
Its quality score is 81.4 while popularity is just 45.8; the repository reports 981 recent commits, 77 releases, and a commit on the as-of date.

risks.text: The product is a relatively broad assistant platform, so adoption may depend on users wanting its particular local daemon, task model, and provider setup.

proven_wrong_if: Its quality-adjusted adoption fails to grow despite sustained releases and active contributions.
The local-first workspace model does not retain users beyond experimentation.

cards.pitch: A remarkably polished, almost undiscovered Rust toolkit that solves concrete rekordbox-to-CDJ workflow gaps.

case.text: Bake'n Deck has a sharply defined use case: measured loudness gain, compound key+BPM sorting, CDJ-safe transcoding, and direct USB export without replacing rekordbox.
It is the strongest popularity/quality mismatch in the shortlist: popularity 4.2 versus quality 80.6, alongside 65 releases and 53,762 README characters.

risks.text: The addressable audience is specialized and depends on rekordbox exports and Pioneer CDJ workflows; the README explicitly positions it as a supplement rather than a replacement for rekordbox.

proven_wrong_if: Usage expands beyond a niche DJ audience into a durable general music-library tool.
Real-world CDJ compatibility and release cadence continue without serious regressions.

cards.pitch: A fast-rising interoperability layer for carrying AI coding sessions across agents, with Rust, JavaScript, WASM, and CLI surfaces.

case.text: txcript converts and searches agent sessions across harnesses, offers native CLI operations such as continue/query/view/crop/export, and exposes Rust, JavaScript, and WASM interfaces.
It pairs momentum 77.1 and newness 83.3 with only 205 stars; the repository also reports nine recent commit authors and a commit on the as-of date.

risks.text: Cross-agent fidelity is inherently uneven: the README qualifies continuation by whether the target supports the carried-over information, and supported harness formats can change.

proven_wrong_if: Major coding-agent vendors converge on incompatible formats that txcript cannot keep up with.
The project gains stars but not repeat usage across multiple agent harnesses.

cards.pitch: A focused, well-released session supervisor that gives coding agents durable PTYs, browser access, and human-in-the-loop control.

case.text: Open Relay keeps the daemon-owned PTY alive after terminal closure, provides terminal and password-protected browser dashboards, supports intervention, and routes work across connected machines.
It has only 109 stars but quality 69.9, 508 commits in 90 days, six recent authors, and 35 releases.

risks.text: The README labels the 0.5.0-beta.3 channel as a breaking preview while stable installs remain on the 0.3 line, so upgrades may require migration care.

proven_wrong_if: The beta-to-stable transition causes enough breakage or churn that users abandon the supervisor.
Persistent sessions and remote intervention do not become a recurring need for agent users.

cards.pitch: A very low-star, security-conscious MCP/LSP bridge that gives AI agents real compiler and IDE semantics instead of guesses.

case.text: mcpls bridges MCP to LSP and exposes 31 tools for type information, references, diagnostics, refactoring, hierarchies, formatting, and symbol search across language servers.
Its popularity is only 16.7, yet quality is 62.0 with 210 recent commits, five recent authors, 20 releases, and a documented security/trust model.

risks.text: Language servers execute workspace code and are not sandboxed; the README explicitly warns users to consult its security guidance before analyzing untrusted code.

proven_wrong_if: MCP clients do not adopt richer compiler-aware workflows beyond basic text retrieval.
The unsandboxed language-server model blocks safe deployment in the environments that need it most.

ranking.note: Best quality/visibility imbalance; 81.4 quality and 981 recent commits. [c_004]
Most under-discovered quality outlier: 4.2 popularity versus 80.6 quality. [c_005]
Best interoperability momentum/newness combination among the low-to-mid popularity group. [c_007]
Strong practical utility and quality at 109 stars, with 508 recent commits. [c_006]
Most neglected specialist pick: 79 stars, 62.0 quality, and unusually clear documentation. [c_010][c_020]
Exceptional momentum and breadth, but already at 372 stars and 70.8 popularity. [c_008][c_018]
High-quality and fast-moving, but 505 stars and 79.2 popularity make it less overlooked. [c_009][c_019]
Very strong momentum, but quality is only 59.1 and the utility is narrower. [c_012]
New and interesting agent workspace, but quality is 49.5 on only 54 recent commits. [c_011][c_021]
Excellent momentum/newness, but specialized market scope and quality 51.6 add execution risk. [c_013]

args.summary: Five Rust developer-tool sleepers stand out. Holon is the best overall quality compounder; baken is the clearest extreme value/visibility mismatch; txcript is the strongest rising interoperability bet; open-relay is a practical session-supervision utility; and mcpls is the most neglected technical specialist. Muxin, pixtuoid, ttfx, Cydonia, and idx are credible alternatives, but their popularity, narrower scope, or lower quality scores weaken the sleeper case.
